extracted.intended_audience: teachers and school administrators (teachers of young pupils; principals of large schools)
extracted.subtask_description: A practical system for governing a large schoolroom: a single explicit rule (the Study Card) that regulates silence/study vs. permitted communication, a daily schedule with timed recitations and exercises, and a moral-discipline approach based on trust, confession, and conscience rather than formal punishments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study Card as the single rule
rubrics_metrics.description: There is but one rule of this school: the Study Card (a plate labeled "Study Hours" that can be up, half down, or down) governs permitted behavior: when it is up (words "STUDY HOURS" presented) it is the signal for silence and study (no communication and no leaving of seats except at the direction of teachers); when half down each scholar may leave her seat and whisper but must not disturb others; when down all duties are suspended and scholars have liberty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immediate and instantaneous compliance when the Card moves: stop speaking, return to seat, and 'forget in your own silent and solitary studies'. All forms of communication (whispering, signs, writing, bowing, any mental intercourse) are forbidden when Study Card is up. The apparatus is used with a bell to give notice of its motion. The system was chosen and adjusted by scholars (they voted frequency). Expect initial difficulty but eventual pleasure in the strict operation of system.

rubrics_metrics.name: No asking teachers for permission (permission protocol)
rubrics_metrics.description: Scholars must never ask the principal or teachers for permission to leave their seats or to whisper; leaving seats or speaking is only right when done at the 'direction' of the teachers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear distinction between a teacher's direction (allowed) and mere consent/permission (not allowed). Examples: being asked by a teacher to bring work = acting under direction (right); asking for a pencil and receiving consent = wrong. Teachers have no authority to grant permission in study hours; only their unsolicited direction counts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emergency exceptions to rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Scholars may break the Study Card rule when 'some very uncommon occurrence' sufficiently extraordinary makes suspension of rules appropriate (e.g., neighbor fainting, a mother or friend entering the room).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Act on your own responsibility in such emergencies and do not ask permission. Be careful not to abuse the privilege; the cause should be very clear and important (analogous to good behavior in church where people do not speak or leave unless a real emergency exists). Minor discomforts do not justify breaking rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale for the Study Card (prevention of off-topic whispering and promotion of uninterrupted study)
rubrics_metrics.description: The prohibition on communication during certain hours was adopted because allowing whispering 'in relation to her studies' proved to fail — whispering became about subjects foreign to school business and harmed the school.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students chose to have a distinct time for whispering rather than asking permission; the card's intervals were adjusted by vote (from every half hour down for one or two minutes, to once an hour). Benefits include improved intellectual habits, the pleasure of observing profound stillness, and easier enforcement (scholars obey implicitly). Teachers should present the rule as chosen by scholars to encourage buy-in.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation of universal moral duty beyond explicit rules
rubrics_metrics.description: There are many arrangements related to instruction, but few specific rules of conduct; scholars are expected to be kind, respectful to superiors, quiet and orderly, not encroach upon others' rights, not produce disorder, and not waste public property — not because rules specify them, but 'because they are in themselves wrong.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not attempt to enact innumerable rules; instead cultivate conscience and moral principle so pupils discover and obey universal duties. Use anecdotes (e.g., running among desks) to teach pupils to reflect on why actions are wrong, rather than merely labeling them 'against the rule.' Emphasize internal reflection over a long list of prohibitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discipline by confession and moral instruction rather than formal punishments
rubrics_metrics.description: There are no punishments as ordinarily understood; when faults occur the principal addresses the pupil kindly, often by note, to convince her of the fault and to elicit frank reply and sincere amendment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If pupils admit fault and promise to amend, the matter is usually closed; the principal relies on conscience awakening rather than penalties. Severe measures may be used only if all other means fail. Use private confession (notes or conversation) rather than public exposure unless necessary. The plan generally succeeds and misbehavior is rare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of conscience and religious framing of forgiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Forgiveness is framed as a religious matter: the principal says 'I never forgive. I have no power to forgive. God must forgive you when you do wrong'; the school's role is to lead pupils to God for pardon; the principal may 'forget' but not 'forgive.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Link discipline and moral improvement to religious instruction; encourage sincere acknowledgement and spiritual remediation. The principal uses the theological distinction to motivate honest confession and moral growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trust-based self-governance (leave teachers' presence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Great confidence is placed in scholars: the school can be left unattended (teachers meeting) and order will prevail as much as when teachers are present — scholars look to the Study Card, not the teacher's presence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This trust cultivates scrupulous and faithful behavior; occasional irregularities occur but are resolved by confession and reform. Teachers should model trust and expect scholars to reciprocate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure for handling discovered misconduct (private acknowledgment and notes)
rubrics_metrics.description: When something wrong is done, the principal states the case and requests those responsible to inform her — sometimes by notes — and they always do; the plan always succeeds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage private acknowledgments rather than public naming. Use moral reasoning to make culprits aware of the extent of harm (e.g., asking those who were inconvenienced to rise) and invite voluntary confession. Non-confession leads to self-reproach; the principal leverages conscience to secure reform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of public exposure unless necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Exposure of faults should be private unless it is necessary to make them public; the principal will not name offenders publicly unless required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public naming risks shaming unnecessarily; prefer private notes/conversation to obtain sincere acknowledgements which restore peace and remove the wrongdoing's effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Schedule the day in half-hour divisions with a posted personal weekly schedule
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide each scholar a blank schedule divided in half-hour slots for a week; scholars fill in their own employments for every half hour so the schedule forms a 'map of the week.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This personal timetable helps pupils find duties at any time and encourages preparation. The teacher provides a standard schedule template (diagram) which shows the institution's divisions and subjects so pupils know how to allocate their time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opening rituals: bell, prayer, hymn, posture
rubrics_metrics.description: Opening is timed: a regulator rings a bell five minutes before start and one minute before; at the moment the Study Card is drawn up and its bell sounds, scholars recline their heads upon desks and join in a short prayer, then sing one or two verses of a hymn led by piano.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow scholars to sit during prayer for comfort but expect uniform and serious posture to produce the proper solemn aspect. Compliance is voluntary and relies on internal motivation rather than surveillance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and use of bells for recitations and transitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Every study hour is divided into two equal halves; a bell is rung five minutes before the close of each half to notify teachers that time is nearly expired and again at the time to call the next class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use bells consistently at five minutes before the end and at the exact end of halves and hours; the Study Card is also moved (half down or up) with associated bell signals to mark the beginning/end of silent study and recesses. These signals ensure smooth, prompt transitions across many classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure and purposes of specific periods (First Hour, Languages, Mathematics, General Exercises, Recess)
rubrics_metrics.description: The day is organized into named periods: First Hour (Evening Lessons — geography, history, natural and intellectual philosophy, natural history); Second Hour (Languages — Latin, French, English as a language); General Exercises (quarter-hour G. for lectures, reading, Bible class, or business); Recess (quarter-hour R. for recreation); Third Hour (Mathematics — arithmetic, algebra, geometry); Second General Exercise includes business and reading the secretary's journal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan varied activities: alternate recitations with general exercises and recesses. Use G. periods flexibly for instruction, moral talks, or administrative business. Recess amusements should be orderly (battledoors, soft balls, marching to piano), and controlled by signals (whistle) to maintain decorum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dividing recitation classes within hour halves
rubrics_metrics.description: Within each hour some classes recite in the first half and others in the second; the bell system signals when classes should take seats and when new classes should come forward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize teachers and classes so recitations rotate predictably; ring the bell five minutes before close to prepare current classes and again at the close to switch classes without confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative recordkeeping and student officers (secretary reads journal)
rubrics_metrics.description: During the business General Exercise, a student (secretary) reads a journal recording notices, arrangements, subjects discussed and decided, and everything important from the preceding day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use student officers to record and communicate school business; this practice engages pupils in governance, preserves institutional memory, and provides a structured forum for school matters.
